opus-5.5.text:
I think there's still quite a lot of room, honestly. If you look at the last several years, a big chunk of the speedup we've seen in inference hasn't come from one thing. It's come from hardware, from lower precision, and from software and algorithms all compounding on each other.

On the hardware side, a few trends are pretty clear. First, numerics. We went from FP32 to FP16 and BF16, then FP8, and now people are serious about FP4 and other microscaling formats. Each step roughly doubles throughput for the same silicon area and power, and we've learned that models are surprisingly robust to lower precision if you're careful about scaling and where you keep higher precision. I don't think we've hit the floor there yet, especially for inference.

Second, inference is often limited not by compute but by memory bandwidth. When you're decoding one token at a time, you're constantly moving weights and the KV cache from memory to the compute units, and the arithmetic intensity is low. So a lot of the gains will come from more HBM bandwidth, bigger on-chip SRAM, and better interconnect, so you can shard across many chips without communication becoming the bottleneck. That's why you see so much interest in different architectures. Some keep everything in SRAM, some use wafer-scale designs, and others build chips specialized for transformer inference.

Third, there's specialization. GPUs have gotten more specialized over time. Tensor cores, the Transformer Engine, asynchronous data movement units. As workloads converge on a few architectures, you can afford to bake more of that into silicon. That trades flexibility for efficiency, and for inference at massive scale that trade can make sense.

But I'd emphasize that hardware alone doesn't get you there. The hardware gives you peak numbers, and then there's often a big gap between peak and what real workloads achieve. That's where a lot of my own work has been, with things like FlashAttention. The point there was that attention wasn't compute bound. It was memory bound, and by being IO-aware you could get big speedups on the same hardware. Every new generation of chips opens that gap up again, because new features need new kernels, new scheduling, new ways of overlapping compute and data movement. So hardware and software co-design is going to matter even more.

Then on the model side, architecture changes help hardware efficiency too. Mixture of experts, state space models and hybrid architectures, and things like speculative decoding all reduce the memory or compute you need per token. When you combine all of that, I'd be surprised if we didn't see another order of magnitude or more in cost per token over the next few years. Probably more, given how much demand there is and how much money is going into it.

So my short answer is that we're nowhere near done. The easy wins from just scaling up FLOPs are getting harder. But between precision, memory systems, specialization, and co-design with the software and the models, there's a lot of runway left.

r001.rationale: The response says workloads are converging on a few architectures, making it feasible to build more inference specialization into chips.

r002.rationale: It mentions sharding across many chips and the need for better interconnect, but does not explain that sharding is needed to accommodate model parameter storage.

r003.rationale: It predicts an order of magnitude or more improvement in cost per token over several years from combined hardware, software, and model changes; it gives no estimate of hardware-only speedup of roughly 2–3× in one year.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's still a lot left, honestly. People sometimes assume we're close to the ceiling because Moore's Law has slowed down, but if you look at where inference actually spends its time, the bottleneck is almost never raw compute. It's memory bandwidth and, increasingly, the interconnect between chips.

For decode, the step where you're generating one token at a time, you're basically loading the weights and the KV cache from memory for every token. The arithmetic you do per byte loaded is tiny. So the number that matters is how fast you can move bytes from HBM into the compute units, and that number has been improving a lot slower than FLOPs have. That gap is exactly why things like FlashAttention mattered: the whole trick was to avoid going to memory as much as possible. On the hardware side, HBM3E to HBM4 is a real jump, and I think we'll keep seeing memory bandwidth grow, but it's expensive, and it's the thing everyone is fighting over.

The second place is interconnect. Once models don't fit on one device, or once you want to batch a lot of users together for mixture-of-experts models, you're shuffling activations and expert outputs between GPUs constantly. NVLink and the rack-scale designs like NVL72 are a big deal there because they make a whole rack look more like one giant chip. I think there's a lot of headroom in that direction: bigger coherent domains, better collectives, hardware that understands the communication patterns of MoE instead of treating it as generic all-to-all.

Then there's precision. We went from FP16 to FP8, and now FP4 is starting to be a real thing in Blackwell. Every time you halve the bits you roughly double your effective bandwidth and double your throughput on the matmul units. The question is how far that can go before quality degrades, and I think the answer is further than people expect, especially with smarter quantization schemes and training that's aware of the low precision from the start.

The last thing I'd say is that hardware and algorithms have to co-design. Attention looks the way it does partly because of what GPUs are good at. If hardware moves toward much larger on-chip SRAM, or more flexible dataflow, that changes which architectures are efficient, and we'd design models differently. So I don't think of it as hardware improvements alone. The really big wins come when you change the algorithm and the hardware at the same time, and we're nowhere near done on that front.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hardware and algorithm co-design, but does not say that increasing model-architecture stability enables chip designers to specialize inference hardware.

r002.rationale: It says models that do not fit on one device require moving activations and expert outputs between GPUs, making interconnect important.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate of a 2–3× inference speedup from hardware improvements within one year.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room, but it depends on which part of inference we’re talking about. When you process the prompt, you have a lot of tokens to work on at once, so you can use the compute on the GPU quite efficiently. When you’re generating tokens one at a time, especially at small batch sizes, you’re often limited by how fast you can read the model weights from memory. More arithmetic throughput alone doesn’t solve that.

So I’d look at memory bandwidth, memory capacity, and the communication between chips, alongside compute. Lower precision is also exciting because it can help on both sides: you move fewer bytes and can do more operations.

The interesting thing is that hardware and algorithms aren’t independent. If we change how we run inference—through batching, quantization, or speculative decoding—we change what we need from the hardware. I think there’s substantial potential left, but realizing it means designing the hardware and the software together.

r002.rationale: It mentions communication between chips, but does not explain that distributing a model to fit its parameter storage makes inter-chip networking more important.

r003.rationale: It says substantial potential remains, but gives no estimate of a 2–3× speedup or a one-year timeframe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room, but it depends on which part of inference you’re looking at. When you’re processing the prompt, you can often use a lot of the GPU’s compute. When you’re generating tokens one at a time, especially at small batch sizes, you’re often limited by how quickly you can move the model’s weights out of memory. Adding more compute alone doesn’t necessarily make that faster.

So I’m excited about improvements in memory bandwidth, the amount of memory you can put close to the compute, and communication between chips. Lower precision is another opportunity: if you can move fewer bits while maintaining model quality, you can improve both speed and energy efficiency.

But I think the biggest gains come from designing the hardware and algorithms together. Can you organize the computation so that you reuse data more and move it less? That’s the motivation behind work like FlashAttention. There’s still substantial headroom there, beyond just waiting for the next generation of GPUs.
